articles.title: 6 useful things to donate before back-to-school season this year

The post 6 useful things to donate before back-to-school season this year first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Back-to-school season is a great time to donate. Kids have outgrown things. Backpacks didn’t survive the year. Notebooks never got opened. Most of it ends up in the trash, and a smaller portion ends up at Goodwill, where it’s gone in days.

“The school year can impose a significant strain on the family budget,” says Stacy Taylor, a marketing specialist at Goodwill Industries of Central Florida, “and with the rising cost of new goods, it can be a challenge for families to give their kids something trendy and stylish, but also useful and useable.”

That’s the gap donations fill. And the weeks before school starts are when Goodwill needs them most.

6 useful items to donate before back-to-school season

Clothes and shoes

Kids’ clothing and shoes are always the first ask. School uniforms, sneakers, gym shorts, jeans, polos, graphic tees, jackets, sweaters, sweatshirts. Truly anything gently worn is fair game.

Taylor notes that thrifted school clothes make practical sense for families: “If they get dirty or worn out by recess, outgrown, or just unwanted, these items are more cost-effective to donate and replace than just buying new.”

This is especially true for kids who are still growing fast. Buying secondhand and donating back when something no longer fits keeps the cycle moving without the guilt of throwing out something that still has wear in it.

Bags and lunchboxes

Gently used backpacks, lunchboxes, and bags go fast this time of year. Messenger bags and laptop bags are in demand too, especially as older kids head into middle and high school.

Check the zippers and straps before donating. If it’s functional, someone will use it.

Water bottles and travel mugs

Reusable water bottles, travel mugs, and coffee tumblers are a quiet hit at Goodwill around back-to-school time. Teachers, in particular, stock up on these in August before the school year kicks off. A water bottle you haven’t used in six months is one a teacher can put to daily use.

School supplies

School supplies are worth going through before you toss them. New or barely touched markers, colored pencils, and crayons can go. So can unused notebooks, binders, and gently used pencil sharpeners. If there’s a pen you grabbed from a conference bag and never opened, add it to the pile.

Goodwill also takes learning toys and Montessori-style materials kids have aged out of, as well as academic books from past school years. Taylor adds: “We’ll even take participation trophies.”

Dorm room items

For anyone clearing out a spare room, or parents whose kids have already headed to campus: mini refrigerators, blenders, toasters, and coffee makers are what college students hunt for in August. They’re expensive new and move quickly at thrift prices.

Make sure everything is clean, working, and has all its cords and parts. Goodwill can’t resell items that are missing components or clearly non-functional.

Why right now

Families are shopping now, not in a month. The same lunchbox nobody wanted at a May yard sale will be gone from a Goodwill shelf in three days.

Most of what ends up in the back-to-school trash pile is still useful. It’s just outgrown. Donating takes about as long as bagging it up for the curb.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought
articles.summary: Makers of some of France's most famous cheeses get waivers on where herds graze due to the lack of grass.
articles.content:
France has temporarily relaxed rules for making some of its best-known cheeses after the summer drought drastically reduced the amount of grass available to feed milk herds.

Government decrees to grant dispensations to manufacturers of Abondance, Beaufort and Comté cheeses - which come from mountains in eastern France - appeared on Wednesday.

Several other cheeses are expected to receive similar waivers, allowing farmers to feed livestock with grass and hay brought in from outside their strict geographical zone.

These include Cantal, Bleu d'Auvergne, Fourme d'Ambert, Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, Reblochon and the goats cheese Rocamadour.

The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for other protected produce because of the effects of the summer heat.

Products that will benefit include some types of Calvados and cider from Normandy, Crémant d'Alsace fizzy wine, lamb from Poitou-Charentes, and Reine-Claude plums.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a positive adaptive policy response by the French government to support traditional cheese producers facing challenges from climate-induced drought. This action helps preserve cultural heritage and supports agricultural livelihoods, benefiting a broad segment of society. The story is focused and provides sufficient detail on the waivers and affected products.
articles.personality_title: France eases cheese rules to help farmers during drought
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – France is known for its famous cheeses, many of which come from specific mountain regions where cows and goats graze on local grass. This summer, a long drought caused a big shortage of grass, making it hard for farmers to feed their animals the usual way.

**What happened** – To help cheese makers, the French government temporarily changed rules that usually say animals must eat only local grass. Now, farmers making cheeses like Abondance, Beaufort, and Comté can feed their animals with grass and hay brought in from other places. Other cheeses such as Cantal, Bleu d'Auvergne, and Reblochon will also get similar exceptions soon. This change was officially approved on Wednesday by the National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which protects the special names of French products.

**Impact** – These temporary rules help farmers keep making traditional cheeses even when nature doesn’t cooperate. It protects the unique taste and quality of these cheeses by allowing farmers to continue feeding their animals properly. It also supports farmers’ incomes and helps keep French food traditions alive during tough weather conditions.

**What's next step** – The government may extend these temporary rules if drought conditions continue. More food products, like certain wines, lamb, and plums, may also get similar help to deal with the effects of the heat and dry weather.

**One-sentence takeaway** – France has relaxed strict cheese-making rules to help farmers feed their animals during drought, protecting both tradition and livelihoods.
articles.personality_title_fr: La France assouplit les règles du fromage pour aider les agriculteurs pendant la sécheresse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La France est célèbre pour ses fromages, souvent produits dans des régions montagneuses où les animaux paissent l’herbe locale. Cet été, une longue sécheresse a fortement réduit la quantité d’herbe disponible, compliquant l’alimentation des troupeaux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pour aider les producteurs, le gouvernement français a temporairement modifié les règles qui obligent normalement à nourrir les animaux uniquement avec de l’herbe locale. Désormais, les éleveurs de fromages comme l’Abondance, le Beaufort et le Comté peuvent donner à leurs animaux de l’herbe et du foin venus d’autres régions. D’autres fromages, comme le Cantal, le Bleu d’Auvergne et le Reblochon, bénéficieront bientôt de mesures similaires. Ces changements ont été approuvés mercredi par l’Institut National de l’Origine et de la Qualité (INAO), qui protège les appellations françaises.

**Impact** – Ces règles temporaires permettent aux agriculteurs de continuer à produire leurs fromages traditionnels même en cas de conditions climatiques difficiles. Elles préservent la qualité et le goût unique de ces fromages, tout en soutenant les revenus des éleveurs et la richesse des traditions françaises.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement pourrait prolonger ces mesures si la sécheresse continue. D’autres produits, comme certains vins, agneaux et prunes, pourraient aussi bénéficier d’aides similaires face à la chaleur et au manque d’eau.

**En une phrase** – La France a assoupli ses règles de fabrication de fromage pour aider les éleveurs à nourrir leurs animaux pendant la sécheresse, protégeant ainsi traditions et moyens de vie.
articles.personality_title_es: Francia flexibiliza las normas del queso para ayudar a los agricultores durante la sequía
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Francia es famosa por sus quesos, muchos de los cuales se producen en regiones montañosas donde las vacas y cabras pastan hierba local. Este verano, una sequía prolongada redujo mucho la cantidad de hierba disponible, dificultando la alimentación de los animales.

**Qué pasó** – Para apoyar a los productores de queso, el gobierno francés cambió temporalmente las reglas que normalmente exigen que los animales coman solo hierba local. Ahora, los agricultores que producen quesos como Abondance, Beaufort y Comté pueden alimentar a sus animales con hierba y heno traídos de otros lugares. Otros quesos como Cantal, Bleu d’Auvergne y Reblochon también recibirán pronto estas excepciones. El Instituto Nacional de Origen y Calidad (INAO), que protege los nombres de los productos franceses, aprobó estos cambios el miércoles.

**Impacto** – Estas reglas temporales ayudan a los agricultores a seguir haciendo quesos tradicionales aunque el clima sea difícil. Protegen el sabor y la calidad de los quesos, además de apoyar los ingresos de los agricultores y mantener vivas las tradiciones alimentarias francesas.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno podría extender estas reglas si la sequía continúa. Otros productos, como ciertos vinos, corderos y ciruelas, también podrían recibir ayuda para enfrentar el calor y la falta de agua.

**Resumen en una frase** – Francia ha relajado las estrictas normas para la producción de queso para ayudar a los agricultores a alimentar a sus animales durante la sequía, protegiendo tradiciones y medios de vida.
